title: Quantitative Results: Collective Action and Violence Prevention
text:
This section presents the quantitative findings from my dissertation, focusing on how agricultural cooperative membership and peasant associations relate to conflict-related victimization in rural Colombia. I use panel data (2016–2022) at the municipality level to examine long-term patterns of collective action and their association with violence.
The analysis includes a Between Effects regression model, which captures how average levels of cooperative membership across municipalities relate to average levels of victimization over time.

Andrea Dávila Saad – Research Portfolio
text:
Welcome to my portfolio. I am a data-oriented political scientist with expertise in quantitative and mixed-methods research applied to conflict studies, institutional trust, and inclusive development. My work is grounded in the belief that rigorous, context-sensitive data analysis is essential to understanding and addressing complex social problems.



I specialize in designing and implementing research strategies that bridge quantitative rigor with qualitative insight. My doctoral dissertation at Virginia Tech analyzed how agricultural cooperatives and peasant associations contribute to violence prevention and peacebuilding in Colombia’s rural municipalities.
Core methodologies I use include:

🧮 Multivariate and multilevel regression models

⚖️ Quasi-experimental and observational designs

🧠 Reflexive thematic analysis

🗺️ Spatial data visualization (GIS)

🧾 Survey design and data cleaning

This skillset allows me to navigate between macro-level datasets (e.g., municipal indicators, ACLED, DANE, UARIV) and micro-level qualitative material (e.g., interviews, testimonies), producing integrated insights for both academic and applied audiences.

## 🔬 Recent and Ongoing Projects

🔗 Collective Action and Peacebuilding
Mixed-methods statistical and thematic analysis of violence and economic alternatives in Colombia
📈 Business and Social Inclusion
Survey-based study of employer attitudes toward ex-combatants, migrants, and victims in Colombia (2021–2023)
📊 Quantitative Results – BE Model
Panel regression results on cooperative membership and conflict-related victimization (2016–2022)





Beyond academia, I support NGOs and institutions in translating data into actionable insights.
At Fundación Ideas para la Paz (FIP), I’ve led and supported multi-stakeholder evaluations and tool development, including:

📊 Trust and institutional performance indices at the municipal level

🧾 Mixed-method diagnostics for early warning response

📉 Surveys measuring employer engagement with peace-related hiring policies

📰 See also: “Medir con enfoque mixto mejora la construcción de paz”
I prioritize transparent documentation, replicable analysis, and ethical use of sensitive data.




I co-founded MAPEA, a research initiative dedicated to applied social analysis in post-conflict and development settings. Through MAPEA, I’ve designed tools, evaluated public programs, and contributed to policy debates around land, reintegration, and territorial governance.

title: Collective Action and Peacebuilding in Rural Colombia
text:
My doctoral dissertation explores how peasant associations and agricultural cooperatives contribute to violence prevention and peacebuilding in rural Colombia. I use a mixed-methods approach combining municipal-level data with testimonies and a regional case study of Sur del Tolima.
The work is grounded in the agrarian question and theories of collective action and civilian agency, drawing on both qualitative and quantitative sources to understand how rural communities organize in the face of violence.
Keywords: collective action, peacebuilding, cooperatives, Colombia, conflict, rural development

title: Collective Action and Peacebuilding in Rural Colombia
text:
Methodological Approach

Quantitative analysis (2016–2022):
Using municipality-year panel data, I analyze trends in victimization and their relationship with forms of collective organization, focusing on PDET vs. non-PDET municipalities.
Key variables include:

Dependent: violence (victimization rate, UARIV)
Independent: agricultural cooperative membership rate and peasant association activity
Controls: municipal capacity, added value, armed actor presence, and ethnic institutions

Qualitative analysis:
I analyzed 16 testimonies from the Colombian Truth Commission and conducted a regional case study in Sur del Tolima, a rural area with high cooperative density and conflict history.
Thematic codes include:

Strategic noncooperation

Social cohesion and trust

Economic alternatives and territorial anchoring

title: Collective Action and Peacebuilding in Rural Colombia
text:
Key Findings

📉 Cooperative membership and victimization: Municipalities with higher average rates of cooperative membership tend to experience lower levels of conflict-related victimization.
🧱 Peasant associations strengthen grassroots governance and help communities resist armed group pressures.
🌱 Cooperatives function as economic peacebuilding platforms, offering both income and identity.
🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Social cohesion and trust networks—built around cooperatives, religious groups, and cultural practices—play a crucial role in community resilience.

These findings suggest that collective action not only improves livelihoods but also enhances a community’s capacity for civilian agency and violence prevention.

title: Collective Action and Peacebuilding in Rural Colombia
text:
More on the Quantitative Evidence
To complement the qualitative insights, I estimated a Between Effects regression model using municipal averages from 2016–2022. The results support the hypothesis that higher cooperative membership is associated with lower violence—particularly in conflict-affected (PDET) municipalities.
📊 For visualizations, model outputs, and R code, see the Quantitative Results Technical Appendix.
